5045.prule: Stress on the first syllable of the radical (root) or stem, i.e. on the first syllable after the nominal/pronominal/verbal prefix string; stated once, hedged ('seems to be'), with no examples and no stress marks in the transcriptions. 5045.idn: the Isiinkere dialect of Wongo (C 85; 'language of the lower area', regarded by the Wongo as the basic dialect, 'true Wongo'); Glottolog 5.3 divides wong1247 into Central, Northern and Southern Wonk (cent2386, nort3380, sout3356), none of which the source's dialect name can be matched to, so the record stays on…
5045.tone: Wongo is described as a tone language throughout: convention 9 'H stands for HIGH TONE' and convention 19 'In phonetic transcriptions, high tones are not marked, except on syllabic nasals' (p. 281, Persée scan); examples carry grave/acute tone marks; remark 6 (p. 283) refers to 'low-toned u'; sec. 2.11 'Tonal behaviour of words' (pp. 292-294) sets up Non-Predicative Tone (NPTONE) vs Predicative Tone (PTONE) shapes of words in sentences, 'PTONE is obtained by raising the first syllable if it is low-toned'. Stress is mentioned only in the one hedged remark 7 and is treated as separate from tone; no interaction between stress and tone is described. Tshiamala 1977 (a generative study of Wongo tone, unpublished UNAZA mémoire) was not reachable.

5049.tone: Hashimoto 1971: 7 phonetic / 4 phonological tones; stress mentioned once, as a device explaining the tone change of yang-p'ing (12) and yang-ch'ü (15) to high falling in non-initial position of compounds ('unless the syllable carries primary stress'; 'composite nouns normally carry primary stress on their first syllables'). Wen 2026 (pp. 2-3): 'Shanghai Wu is regarded as having left-headed word stress; the unstressed (i.e., non-initial) syllables undergo tonal deletion, while the underlying tone of the stressed syllable is preserved' (citing Chen 2000, Duanmu 1993, 1995), but for Shaoxing Wu 'no independent acoustic correlates of stress beyond tonal patterns themselves' (p. 111) and the stress account is called circular. tn.quote: Wutung tone is lexical, the domain of operation of phonemic tone being the whole word, with tone ‘melodies’ applying to the entire word and being realised as pitch levels on each syllable. There are four tonal melodies, H (high), L (low) and HL (fall, comprising the sequence [h-l] attached to a single syllable) and LHL (comprising the sequence [l-h-l]). ... While the tone-bearing unit is the word, the level at which the surface pitches are realised is the syllable.

tn.note: Four word-tone melodies (H, L, HL fall, LHL) built from [h]/[l] elements, mapped left-to-right with an optional tone-attracting accent; no tonal morphemes; stress non-contrastive and free-varying.

5055.prule: Fixed left-edge accent on every free morpheme/word: the accent (higher pitch + greater intensity) sits on the initial mora in words of 1-3 morae and covers the first two morae in words of 4+ morae; the accented stretch contrasts in pitch with all following syllables. 5056.prule: SIL tradition (McLeod & Mitchell 1977; Hall 1979 after Burgess ms.): stress predictable and non-contrastive; in words with only short vowels the final syllable is stressed with alternating stresses leftward (2σ final; 3σ 1st+last; 4σ 2nd+last); long syllables (long vowel, V+i, closed) are always stressed; the final syllable of every locução is stressed; diminutive -re never stressed. All three agree stress is predictable; none agree on where it falls.
5056.srule: SIL account: additional stresses on alternate syllables counted leftward from the final (main) stress -- all-short-vowel words 3σ 1st+3rd, 4σ 2nd+4th (McLeod & Mitchell 1977) = Hall 1979:15 'na última sílaba de frases e nas sílabas alternadas que precedem' -- and on every long/closed syllable (with free variation of the short-syllable stresses when heavies are present, Hall). Quintino 2012:163 (own data) likewise: 'acentos secundários que ocorrem em intervalos regulares da direita para a esquerda, nunca em sílabas adjacentes', but quantity-insensitive. Pickering 2010:239 recognises no separate secondary level (rhythm-based level-1 accent after Fox 2000; foot structure undetermined).

conflict.would_settle: Substantively the clash is final(+weight) vs penult(quantity-insensitive); what is unknown is whether both are true of different speech communities/eras. Side 1 rests on 1958-70s SIL fieldwork with near-monolingual (mostly female) speakers of the Culuene dialect area; side 2 on 1980s-2000s speakers of T.I. São Marcos (Lachnitt, Pickering) and Pimentel Barbosa (Quintino), and both modern authors themselves invoke the 50-year gap / Portuguese bilingualism (Quintino 2012:164 fn.26; Pickering 2010:238). It would be settled by (a) the unread primary analysis Burgess 1967 'Length and Stress in Xavante' ms. (SIL Brazil archive / Museu Nacional; bibliography row 12, access unknown) to see whether SIL's 'final' is word stress or the phrase-final boundary prominence that Hall calls 'o acento mais forte' and Pickering equates with Fox's level-2 accent; (b) the unread Salesian grammar Lachnitt 1988 Damreme'uwaimramidzé (bibliography row 11, print only) for a fuller independent rule; and decisively (c) an instrumental study of all-light di- and trisyllables in phrase-medial vs phrase-final and emphatic vs neutral contexts with present-day Culuene (Parabubure) and São Marcos/Pimentel Barbosa speakers, since SIL itself records emphatic lengthening of the penult of a locução and phrase-final penult lengthening in some stems (Aspectos 'Duração enfática'; Pequeno dicionário Apêndice V), which could make one set of facts yield both descriptions.

5057.prule: Stress position is lexically contrastive in polysyllables ending in a high-vowel phoneme (i, e, u; three of Sibe's five vowel phonemes, fn. 6): some words stress the final syllable and keep the vowel (mukú [muˈkʰuː] 'water', cixé 'flea', sisxé 'mattress', χasí 'eggplant', erdé 'morning', dexamé 'mother's sister's husband'), others stress the preceding syllable and delete the (phonologically present, fn. 8) final vowel (muku [mukʷʰ] 'dice face', cixe 'damp', sisxe 'sieve', χasi 'still', erde 'early', jirame [d͡ʑiˈɾam] 'thick'). The author gives no predictor, marks the stress with a lexical acute accent in the phonemic form, calls (13)-(17) minimal pairs by stress position, and states (§5 [2], §7, English abstract) that stress position can be distinctive in Sibe. Default for everything else (a/o/consonant-final words, and the vowel-retaining members of the i/e/u class): the high-pitch-onset stressed syllable is 'as a rule the last syllable' (原則として最後の音節; yila [jɪˈlaː], doχuluN [dɔʁʊˈlun]). The contrast is confined to final vs. penult (right-edge two-syllable window).

5058.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (the whole affixed word counts; diphthongs count as two emic syllables so that the penult rule holds); quantity-insensitive; the stressed vowel is usually lengthened as a consequence of stress. Stress is not contrastive.

5061.heavy: A final syllable that (a) ends in i or u, (b) contains a nasal vowel, (c) contains a diphthong, (d) ends in a consonant, or (e) has its vowel preceded by y or j. Items (b)-(d) are weight conditions (CVV-type: diphthong, nasal vowel; CVC: closed syllable); items (a) and (e) are segmental (final high vowel) and onset (y/j before the final vowel) conditions, not weight.
5061.dflt: Not stated. Penult is implied by 'só há palavras oxítonas e paroxítonas' and shown by most accent-marked -go forms on the same page (p. 16 §3.2: arágo, xikúgo, montógo, kupágo, xabrêgo, uyuíngo, xukégo, jubêgo, lanprêgo, jabrêgo, inbrugúgo, jupegúgo, zmaragúgo, tayegêgo, kré agúgo), but it is not exceptionless: the same list has kringó 'comer', oxytone with a final plain oral -o meeting none of the five conditions, and the p. 18 §5.1 synonym list has more plain-oral-vowel-final oxytones: akrugó 'pequeno', ximbó 'cacete', konkré 'cacete', axó 'olho', mankwé 'negro', kaité 'água', pró 'velho', utxaká 'gambá', makringó and xanduré 'cachimbo'. 5062.dloc: p. 272, §1.2 'Phonotactics, vowel harmony, tone harmony, consonant harmony and stress'.
5062.prule: Word stress on the final syllable of the phonological word (stem + affix; one or two syllables, three only in subject-prefix + disyllabic-stem verb forms), i.e. the strong syllable of the last iambic (weak-strong) foot. No weight condition is stated (closed syllables occur only word-finally anyway: 'The canonic syllable is (C)V(C) word-finally, (C)V elsewhere').

5062.quote: Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabêm phonology. The foot is iambic, that is, in its full form it consists of a sequence of two syllables, the first weak, the second strong. Thus a two-syllable word consists of a full iambic foot. A single-syllable word has one foot but only a strong syllable, and a three-syllable word like /ka-seleŋ/ has two feet, the first (/ka/) with only a strong syllable, the second (/seleŋ/) a full foot. Word stress falls on the final syllable.
5062.loc: p. 272, §1.2 'Phonotactics, vowel harmony, tone harmony, consonant harmony and stress' (the stress sentence is the last sentence of the paragraph beginning 'Within the word, the foot plays a role in Jabêm phonology'). Tone statements: pp. 272 and 274; word/compound definition p. 272.

5062.tone: Two-tone register language. p. 272: 'Jabêm has two tones, high and low, described below.' p. 274: 'The two syllables of a foot have like tone. Tone is either high or low, labelled H and L in the text of this sketch. Tone also determines the voicing of stops. In an H foot any stops are voiceless; in an L foot voiced.'... 'L will be marked orthographically by a grave accent on the vowel of the strong syllable of an L foot'. Tone is a foot-level property coexisting with the final-stress rule; the stress rule is stated separately and explicitly. The older missionary literature denies stress: Zahn 1922 as quoted in Streicher & Zahn 1982: x: 'One must distinguish very carefully between the expressions ‘height of tone’, or pitch and accent. In Jabem we have no accent (stress), but a distinct pitch. (Zahn 1922)' and 'The accents on words in this dictionary are musical tone or pitch accents, not stress accents.'

tn.quote: Au passé immédiat, on constate que le MT en ilaalɛ est constitué de deux éléments ‘bí máa’, par contre en iyaa, il n’est constitué que d’un seul élément ‘maá’. Les deux dialectes ont en commun le morphème ‘maá’ qui subit une différence au niveau du système tonal où l’on remarque en ilaalɛ le ton haut marqué sur V1 et en iyaa sur V2.
tn.translation: In the immediate past, the tense marker in ilaalɛ consists of two elements 'bí máa', whereas in iyaa it consists of a single element 'maá'. The two dialects share the morpheme 'maá', which differs at the level of the tonal system: in ilaalɛ the high tone is marked on V1 and in iyaa on V2.

5067.dq: Ichishkiin has word level stress, with one primary stress per spoken word.
5067.dloc: Jansen 2010, ch. II sec. 2.6 'Stress', pp. 52-57; Figure 2.2 p. 56; Tables 2.10-2.11 pp. 55, 57. Hargus & Beavert 2005 secs. 3.1, 3.3, 5.3 (pp. 65-68, 87-88); Hargus & Beavert 2016 sec. 2 (p. 2) and sec. 3 (p. 3).
5067.heavy: No weight rule. Tendency only (Jansen p. 53): 'A second tendency is that a syllable with a long vowel (CVV) or a CVC syllable will be stressed... Note though, there are exceptions to each of these tendencies... tiichcim [tiichám] 'land, earth, country' has an unstressed long vowel.' H&B 2005 sec. 3.1: 'a greater-than-random attraction of stress to heavy syllables (-VV or -VC)'.
5067.prule: Lexical: every word has exactly one primary stress (raised pitch + greater intensity); within a root its position is unpredictable (any syllable of a root can be stressed; minimal pair pámta / pamtá) and must be learned per word. Statistical tendencies only (initial in CVCV/CVCCV roots; CVV or CVC syllables attract stress; barred-i rarely stressed), each with counterexamples.
5067.srule: None in ordinary words: 'one primary stress per spoken word' (Jansen 2010: 52); 'Words surface with one accent' (Hargus & Beavert 2014: 333); Jacobs 1931: 117 'no secondary stress' in Northwest Sahaptin. A secondary stress (extra energy, no pitch peak) is reported only in trisyllabic-or-longer totally reduplicated iterative verbs, on the reduplicant and the verb stem (Hargus & Beavert 2016 sec. 3-4; none in mono-/disyllabic reduplications); Jansen also hears a slight, speaker-variable secondary stress on inherently stressed applicative suffixes and inverse pá- when another morpheme takes the word stress (pp. 316, 353).

5067.exq_: Some prefixes and suffixes are inherently stressed and will (almost always) receive the word level stress. ... Some roots resist the stress-stealing prefixes (but not the stress-stealing suffixes) and keep the word level stress. I call these 'strong roots' following Hargus and Beavert 2006b. ... It…
5067.tone: No lexical tone. Hargus & Beavert classify Yakima Sahaptin as a pitch-accent language: H&B 2005 sec. 5.3 'pitch-accent appears to be a special case of stress... As reviewed in §3, YS appears to have all of the predicted characteristics of a pitch-accent language, including realization of accent with a predictable pitch contour'; H&B 2016 p. 2 shows Hyman's Obligatoriness and Culminativity both hold ('one and only one syllable is the most prominent'), with accented vs unaccented monosyllables ([kú] 'do' vs [ku] 'and'). Jacobs 1931:117 (carried in H&B 2005 sec. 3.4): 'stress and high tone are one phenomenon in northern Sahaptin'. Phonetic correlates: higher pitch and greater intensity, not duration (H&B 2005 sec. 4). Jansen 2010 describes the same system as 'stress' throughout; coded lexical (unpredictable root accent) rather than tone or pitch accent because the accent is culminative, obligatory and privative and every source treats it as stress/accent, not tone.

5068.dloc: Ch. 3 Phonology, §3.4 'Stress assignment', pp. 57-61 (rule p. 57; non-finality and prefix domain p. 59; clitics, nominalizers =na/=ha, secondary stress and ideophone exception pp. 60-61); §3.5 p. 62 restates the domain.
5068.heavy: Closed syllables: 'Closed syllables, however, attract stress.' Yakkha 'has no distinctions of length or tenseness for vowels' (p. 57), so weight is coda-based only; a domain-final closed syllable is excluded from attracting stress ('the stress never moves to the final syllable, even when the syllable is heavy').
5068.dflt: First syllable of the stress domain (initial stress), e.g. ˈom.phu, ˈko.ko.mek; also when the only closed syllable is final (ˈkho.rek, ˈkam.ni.bak).
5068.prule: Main stress falls by default on the first syllable of the stress domain (stem plus suffixes; prefixes and phrasal clitics are outside the domain). If the domain contains closed syllables, main stress moves to the rightmost closed syllable that is not domain-final (i.e. rightward only as far as the penult); a final closed syllable never attracts stress (ˈkam.ni.bak). Prefixed monosyllabic stems therefore surface with final stress (a.ˈpaŋ ‘my house’).
5068.srule: None detected in simple words: 'It is hard to tell whether there is secondary stress. Even in words with five syllables... no secondary stress could be detected.' In inflected verb forms secondary stress can fall on the verb stem when main stress has moved rightward (ˌndum.men.cu.ˈŋan.na, ˌtum.meʔ.ˈnen.na); in compounds it falls on the first syllable of the second member, with main stress on the compound's first syllable, and may be word-final (ˈko.len.ˌluŋ, ˈsa.meʔ.ˌchoŋ).

5071.heavy: Not a placement condition. The source states a stress-to-weight condition: the nucleus of the stressed syllable of content words is two moras (V: = long modal/laryngealized vowel or diphthong, or VC = V + glottal stop / V + voiceless stop; Figure 25, p. 133), and no content word has a stressed open syllable with a short vowel (p. 166).
5071.prule: No stress-placement rule is stated. Yalálag Zapotec is described as a tone language with three phonemic tones (High, Low, Falling); stress appears only as a presupposed prosodic condition: each content word has one primary-stressed syllable (the root/stem syllable; roots and words are predominantly monosyllabic), that syllable's nucleus is bimoraic (long modal or laryngealized vowel, diphthong, or vowel plus coda), no content word has a stressed open syllable with a short vowel, and only the primary-stressed syllable can bear the Falling contour.

5071.tone: Tone is the contrastive prosody: 'The three phonemic tones, High, Low and Falling, will be represented by accents over the vowels' (p. 10); sec. 4.5 establishes the three-way contrast acoustically, with grammatically conditioned tone changes in stems (e.g. High tone in the potential aspect, p. 11). Stress is never described in its own right (no 'stress'/'accent' heading in the TOC); it is invoked only as the syllable that licenses Falling tone and that must be bimoraic, plus Newberg 1983's report (via Avelino p. 106) that checked vs laryngealized vowels are 'allophones conditioned by tone and stress'. The dissertation gives no minimal pairs, no positional rule, and no phonetic correlates of stress.

tn.quote: Yaldlag Zapotec has three tone heights: High, Low and Falling. Two factors indicate the phonemic status of the three tones, and especially that of the contour tone. First, none can be derived from one of the other two in the lexicon; and second, the three tones are the maximum of tone heights found in the tone system. Nevertheless, it is important to mention that contour tones—Falling and Rising—- and tone adjustments, such as upstep and downstep, might arise as the result of morphological and intonational processes.
